aaData: Often appears with emphatic deverbal noun iparse before in double verb construction, e.g. ex. 131
can mean both 'ask (to/whether)' and 'tell' sense of 'give a request/command'.
Not a verb but an adjective combined with the verb 'be'

This is an experiencer-object verb, taking the ergative form of gers 'hunger' as its stimulus/actor, and the experiencer of hunger as its undergoer. The thing hungered for can be added as a possessor NP before hunger, so that 'hungry for cassowary' is 'cassowary's hunger'. See article. Not considered a valency alternation since this is not at clausal level. No alternations attested.
Experiencer-object construction: stimulus is ergative of enzine 'sickness', plus räms 'make'

Can mean 'hit', 'beat' and 'kill'. krtas can be added to make the 'kill' meaning clear. RR form ägms has undergone some semantic change: it means 'fight' in general (which may involve hitting, but not necessarily) and can also be used with a singular subject, so this is best seen as a lexicalised use of an original reciprocal rather than a fully compositional case.
no direct counterpart

skop upris - Not an exact translation: means 'close eyes' (e.g. as in prayer). Another phrase offered as a non-exact translation equivalent was skop wzne 'it's burning my eyes', e.g. when smoke burns your eyes and make you blink, but this refers to the cause rather than the instantaneous action.
This also means 'make a noise' and 'smart, sting'. The causative meaning counterpart is expressed by the formally unrelated transitive verb zeys 'to cook, to boil' .

When combined with the towards or away prefixes n- and ng-, this is commonly translated by 'bring' or 'take'. Morphological peculiarity: this infinitive has two stems, √renz and √ane. Not yet clear what the difference in meaning between these is. Semantic difference between renzas and wazrs needs checking. Note also that renzas contrasts with a further verb menzas 'lead'. This contrast is a bit like French apporter vs amener - there are dimensions of whether the object is non-human (renzas) or human (menzas), which is the first difference speakers point out, but also the choice reflects a difference between carrying (renzas) and leading (menzas). Nonetheless, menzas is still used of some situations (e.g carrying someone in a car) which are better construed as carrying than leading.

Other meanings expressed by passives, resultatives etc. in English are expressed by infinitive constructions, such as: Mngw räms mái ym. - The house is still being built. Mngw rämsmne ym. - The house has been built. Yna mngw wgd rämsmne ym. - This house is well-built.
Nuance of 'flare up, catch fire'. The causative version wizers differs from other causatives in having an apparent diathetic prefix i-.

Though some of its semantic range is better covered by 'lead' than 'carry', it is included here because there is some spillover, mediated by its uses in 'bring' and 'take' contexts with human objects. Perhaps best translated as 'cause to move along with one, of a human object'

Given as second meaning of verb wazrs, first offered as translation of 'pour'.
Basically means 'ascend (by whatever means)'; can combine with directional prefixes to mean 'come up', 'go up' etc. Regularly used to describe entry into house (which involves climbing up a ladder)

Covers 'cook (on fire)' and 'boil', like German kochen, but not cooking in ground oven, which is dus (also a transitive verb apparently, but no inflected forms attested). Note the autobenefactive form ozs 'cook for oneself'.
cook in ground oven (so far only attested as infinitive)
momae ke otärs
otärs is simply 'to make a noise'; 'cough' is obtained by conjoining this with the phrase momae ke 'mucus noise' here functioning as a coverb
Usually accompanied by cognate object e 'crying'.

Middle form is eñps; in the transitive infinitive form, the nasal depalatalises in initial position, though the root is still (a)ñp. Also, there are two attested infinitives, nps and eñps, both transitive: it looks like one means 'cut up' and the other 'cut, make an incision in'. At present these have not been entered as alternations, but more data may warrant this. Other semantically related verbs, not entered here since they pattern similarly, are pos 'cut/chop', tenas 'butcher'
kr 'death' plus appropriately inflected form of 'to be'
Irregular infinitive, same as noun for 'food' and 'yam'
Experiencer object construction. If the stimulus is expressed, it will be as an adjunct taking the source suffix -mne.
The RR form awaets can be taken literally ('follow each other') but can also be used of a courting or mating couple.

This is a phrasal construction, made up of the predicate adjective brbr-ba 'fear-with' plus the transitive verb wets 'to make', thus 'A make P with-fear'. 'To be frightened of, fear' is brbr plus the verb 'to be'.
So far no infinitive has been obtained for this verb.

This verb is, etymologically, räms 'do' plus the benefactive prefix wa-, thus 'do for'. Particularly if a directional prefix is used, it is possible to use the unprefixed form 'do' with the meaning 'give', e.g. 'do hither'.

This is an irregular infinitive; stem is -m (nondual) / -ren (dual). Both go and come are directional forms of 'be': thus -ngm 'go; be hither (non-dual)', -nm 'come, be hither (non-dual)'. The goal can readily be omitted, and other adjuncts are also possible (e.g. perlative, if saying 'go [by this path]'.
Means 'scrape' (e.g. sago) rather than pound; likewise the other near-translation term offered (not eneteed) is értes which means 'pound' more than grind. Infin. needs verification.

Can mean both 'hear' and 'listen', also 'understand'. The transitive construction, though formally basic to the other two alternations, is actually rarer than the middle object-downgrading construction.
Clausal complements of the type 'help to climb a ladder' etc are expressed as infinitives plus the locative.

Though the basic meaning of this verb is 'hide', in some contexts the verb wérnis can also mean 'steal'. Note that the source of the stolen goods is specified as a possessive phrase only, so that reciprocals are then coded using the reciprocal pronoun only, rather than the verb-coded reciprocal, which requires that the reciprocant be one of the verbally-indexed arguments in the original frame.

Can mean 'hit', 'beat' and 'kill'. krtas can be added to make the 'kill' meaning clear. RR form ägms has undergone some semantic change: it means 'fight' in general (which may involve hitting, but not necessarily) and can also be used with a singular subject, so this is best seen as a lexicalised use of an original reciprocal rather than a fully compositional case.
Verb means 'to hunt'; it usually combines with the noun ele 'hunting'. 'To be a hunter' is derived from this as an agentive nominalization: ärser är [hunt-NLZR-AG.NL person]
Seems to mean 'jump up and down'
Means 'jump up'; destination can be specified by allative adjunct.

Can mean 'hit', 'beat' and 'kill'. krtas can be added to make the 'kill' meaning clear. This is not a verb but an predicative adjective, and must be combined with the verbs 'to be' or 'to become'. Both of its arguments take the absolutive. Reciprocals (know each other) are formed by using a dual/plural form of 'be', as appropriate, and placing the reflexive/reciprocal pronoun in the object slot. 'Know how to' is expressed also by mete, with a single NP argument plus an infinitive complement taking the allative. 'Know that' is also expressed by mete: the clause representing what is known simply follows, in finite form, with no complementizer or special marking. 'Not know' is expressed by the predicative adjective; mäpna, most likely derived from a form of mete (or its root) by adding privative -pna.
Usually combines with cognate object bén, though not necessarily. (This isn't listed here as part of the valence)

Semantic range like English 'leave' - can be used where agent moves away from patient, or drops off the patient somewhere, or desists from an activity. The derived benefactive form is prefixed with wa, with the o changing to w (thus or > wawr) but the infinitive is the same.
Lit. 'look upon/see with sweetness'. 'Like V-ing' can be expressed by using an infinitive clause in the U position.

Means 'to be sitting', as opposed to amzs 'to assume sitting position, to sit down'. There is another positional form mzngr, which is the one that formally participates in the three-way series with amzs. It can also mean 'live, reside' (at: LOC). 'Live' can also be expressed by various nominal-type expressions, such as yu är 'permanent person' and wirär 'residing person' (the lattter is an agent nominalisation of were).

Means 'load to overflowing', 'fill'. It is the derived causative form of the verb apls 'overflow'. This is an unusual example of the aspectual choice affecting the case frame: it appears that the perfective, which has the meaning 'to overflowing', puts the theme in the absolutive, while the imperfective, which means 'to the brim', puts it in the locative. So far this is the only verb attested like this.

This verb appears to be a causative form of a middle tantum, i.e. assist someone else to get loaded up. The middle counterpart, awags, means 'load oneself up (with: ABS)'. So far no form wags is attested.
Causative form of the infinitive is wewes; middle form is ewes.

Imperfective-oriented verb, opposed to winḡs 'catch sight of'; corresponds variously to 'see, gaze at, look at'. No difference in case-frame or valency-alternation behaviour between these meanings of wakaes.

Other meanings expressed by passives, resultatives etc. in English are expressed by infinitive constructions, such as: Mngw räms mái ym. - The house is still being built. Mngw rämsmne ym. - The house has been built. Yna mngw wgd rämsmne ym. - This house is well-built.

The RR form of the perfective-oriented verb, inḡs meaning 'catch sight of' can be used with the meaning 'meet'; note that for unexpected meetings the β-prefix is used in the past tense instead of the expected α-form.

The only attested infinitive is the middle form äbäts but this can also occur in a transitive frame. The transitive form uses just the root bät, whereas the middle form adds the diathetic prefix ä-. This is therefore a case of defective infinitives rather than any abnormality in the finite forms.

This is a RR verb, also meaning 'end, be within confines' - the rationale for its use with naming is that names stay (are confined within) the clans of the bestower and the named alike. The recipient may be added as a NP taking the oblique plus the locative
semantic range includes 'scratch' (e.g. scratch on mat', or verbs of removing surface by scraping, scaling or peeling. So far this is the closest equivalent to 'peel' that has been recorded.

There is no single verb corresponding to English 'put'. Rather, there are a large number of derived causative expressions, each based on a semantically precise 'positional verb'. Positional verbs are stative in meaning and have no infinitive; from them are derived pairs of dynamic verbs – a causative, meaning 'put in position X' and a middle, meaning 'get into position X'. We use kms as an example here – positional e.g. ykmangr 's/he/it is lying, in a lying position' (no infinitive but various inflected forms' is the positional, and corresponding to it are äkms 'to lie down' and kms 'to put in a lying position'. There are about 35 sets of this type. Transitives of this type optionally take a locative adjunct – not listed here as part of the coding frame, since it is semantically predictable.
Always occurs with the absolutive noun nu 'water; rain'.
There is another transitive verb käns 'roll up' (e.g. rolling up a mat) not included here.

Other related verbs are wanms 'call (s/o s/t)' and wädäräns 'say, gossip, allege'; see N4:59; these are not given here. zi 'word, language' can occur in the absolutive as a cognate object; it can be modified by possessives. The topic of conversation (about X) can be represented by an adjunct in the originative case.
This is a middle tantum form (as indicated by the a- prefix), without a correponding transitive form attested.

Perfective-oriented verb, meaning 'catch sight of'; it has an imperfective-oriented counterpart wakaes, whose meaning refers to stable visual scrutiny 'see (duratively), gaze at, look at'. The RR form of this verb can also be used with the meaning 'meet'; note that for unexpected meetings the β-prefix is used in the past tense instead of the expected α-form.

Imperfective-oriented verb, opposed to winḡs 'catch sight of'; corresponds variously to 'see, gaze at, look at'. No difference in case-frame or valency-alternation behaviour between these meanings of wakaes.

This verb can mean 'send', in which case the T is indexed on the verb, or 'farewell, say farewell to', in which case it is the person being farewelled (sent off), also a T. In the first case, the recipient is coded as a dative adjunct. So far no evidence of this verb taking a benefactive applicative.
This verb means 'send ' (as the first move in an exchange)', in contrast to trärs which means 'send (as part of an ongoing exchange)'.
This verb means 'send (as part of an ongoing exchange)', as contrasted with wäbärs 'send (as the first move in an exchange)'.
SHAVE (a body part/person) [shave-a-body-part_person]
Means 'shout at, to do/not do something'. The cause can be expressed by an adjunct NP followed by dbnan 'because of', or by an adverbial clause introduced by mnegta 'in order to'
means 'shout out to, call out to', e.g. to establish contact

angan 'song' + räms 'to make', forming a transitive construction with fixed object NP (coded here as a transitive). Angan can be modified by other nominal or adjectival material, e.g. marirmarir angan 'love song'. Beneficiary/audience can be added by a dative adjunct.
This verb means 'to sit down, to assume sitting position'.
Root only; no infinitive; participates in placement and assume-position alternations with the verb amzs. Broadly synonymous with the positional erengr.

Means 'to be sitting', as opposed to amzs 'to assume sitting position, to sit down'. 'Live' can also be expressed by various nominal-type expressions, such as yu är 'permanent person' and wirär 'residing person' (the lattter is an agent nominalisation of were).

When used with the meaning 'smell', this takes the noun wimb 'smell' as a coverb; this is typically (though not necessarily) in immediate preverbal position, but does not trigger undergoer agreement. When the meaning is 'sniff, sniff at' this is not included. At present the coverb structure is not listed in the given argument structure.
Wr is basically an action-denoting noun, and can be combined with the light verb äräms 'do' to mean 'steal' (e.g. är wr närämte 'the man is stealing').

kaps means 'take' in the sense of 'pick up'; 'take from' is expressed by kaps conjoined with renzas 'carry', or else by renzas with a source coded as possessive.

Can take 'how to' clause: a finite clause introduced by dene 'thus'. AA alternation gives meaning 'teach'.
This means 'tell, recount' and is especially common for describing the passing on of information, stories etc.
wabaes (tr.) 'think of something'; awabaes (RR) 'think, be mindful, pay attention' [semantically specialized]
Ämbärs and ämbers have also been recorded as variants. Has nuance of 'think about, be preoccupied with, be worried about'.

The meaning 'throw at' is expressed by following this verb by either näms 'throw and hit' or lts 'miss' according to the meaning to be expressed. It appears that the intentional goal (the object thrown at) can only be introduced by an additional verb of hitting or missing.

means 'tie, fasten', also 'hook', i.e. overall 'make fast, attach (together)'. This verb has further metaphorical extensions to 'be (emotionally) attached' (e.g. lovers), 'be committed to' (e.g. to a project).
adjective mñte 'desiderous' plus copula. Can take desire complements that are either infinitives inflected for the allative (e.g. 197) or conditionals introduced by geä.
